title: F2P vs Paid: Pricing and Engagement on Steam
impactStat: Free-to-play games are played a quarter as long as paid ones — 124 median minutes against 530 — and correcting for genre makes the gap wider, not narrower
oneSentenceDescription: A 20,761-game study of whether going free-to-play actually buys engagement on Steam, built to kill the tautology that free things get downloaded more, and to test whether any gap survives comparing like genre with like.
cardDescription: Does going free-to-play actually buy engagement? Across 20,761 Steam games, free titles are played a quarter as long as paid ones — and comparing within genre makes the gap wider, not narrower.
targetIndustryRole: Data Analyst, Data Scientist (gaming, product analytics)

summaryImpact: I set out to test a claim studios act on: that going free-to-play buys engagement. On Steam it does not. Across 20,761 games released since 2015, free games have a median playtime of 124 minutes against 530 for paid ones — a gap of more than four to one. The obvious objection is that free games cluster in genres that are simply played less, so I compared within genre across the 58 genres holding enough of both models. That correction was supposed to shrink the gap. It widened it, from a Cliff's delta of -0.457 to -0.482. The finding is not that the free-to-play advantage is a genre effect. It is that there is no advantage to explain.
problemSpace: A studio choosing a launch pricing model, or a publisher deciding whether to take an ageing paid title free, wants to know what the model buys in engagement. The trap is that the obvious analysis answers a different question: free games have more owners, which is a tautology, because free things get downloaded. The question worth asking is whether players who take a free game stay in it as long as players who paid, and whether any difference holds once you stop comparing a free MOBA against a paid visual novel.
stakeholders: Studio leadership choosing a launch pricing model; publishers weighing a free-to-play conversion for an existing title; live-ops and product teams forecasting engagement from price.
inputs: SteamSpy's full catalogue — 27,021 apps, paged at the documented one-request-per-minute limit — enriched app by app from the Steam storefront for AUD price, genres, release date and the free-to-play flag. 26,017 apps, 52,034 requests, 7 failures. Every response is cached to disk untransformed, so a re-run returns identical data and an interrupted pull resumes instead of restarting. Playtime comes from Steam review payloads: 3,497 games sampled, up to 200 reviewers each.
categoryLeader: Paid games at 60 AUD and above hold a median 2,484 minutes, more than ten times the 233 minutes of games under 10 AUD.
priceBehaviour: Median playtime rises monotonically across every AUD price band: 233 minutes under 10, 630 in 10-30, 1,420 in 30-60, and 2,484 above 60. Price level separates engagement far more cleanly than the free-versus-paid split does.
surprisingPatterns: Free-to-play wins in exactly one genre — Clicker, 530 minutes against 218 — and ties in Idler. Both are built around long passive sessions, and both are places where free-to-play is the native model rather than a discount. Everywhere else paid wins, including MMORPG (1,216 against 2,810), where a free model should have its strongest case.
hypothesisVsReality: I expected the naive gap to be largely a genre artefact: that free-to-play concentrates in genres that play short, and that correcting for genre would collapse the difference. The opposite happened. The genre-adjusted effect size (-0.482) is slightly larger than the naive one (-0.457). Whatever produces the gap, it is not the mix of genres that go free.
deadEnds: The headline metric died mid-project. The plan was SteamSpy's median playtime, which it still serves — as zeroes. All four playtime fields are zero for every one of the 1,000 apps on the first catalogue page, and for both apps I spot-checked. The plain reading is that Steam's profile-privacy changes removed the sample those figures were derived from, leaving the old schema behind. Every playtime option the plan offered died with it, so the metric was rebuilt on per-player playtime from Steam review payloads.
secondaryModel: Concurrent players per owner, computed across the whole 20,761-game cohort as a cross-check on the sampled playtime metric. It agrees on direction (naive -0.109, genre-adjusted -0.092) and independently reproduces the price-band gradient. But 54% of the cohort has a concurrent-player count of exactly zero, so it is mostly ties and cannot carry the headline alone.
executionDeadEnds: Stratifying on Steam's storefront genres would have been a weak correction — they are three broad buckets, and ELDEN RING is simply Action, RPG. SteamSpy's user tags carry the resolution the question needs, but not raw: Dota 2's highest-voted tag is Free to Play at 60,040 votes, three times the next. Ranking by votes would have sorted every free game into a Free to Play stratum and left no cell containing both models — the strata would have restated the variable under test. Business-model tags are therefore excluded by name. Because most high-voted tags are descriptors rather than genres (Difficult, Dark Fantasy, Third Person), genres come from an explicit vocabulary rather than whatever ranks highest. A first pass still put 65% of the cohort into an umbrella bucket like Action or Casual; making specific tags beat umbrellas regardless of votes brought that to 18%.
methodology: Ownership is reported by SteamSpy as a band, never a number, so it is carried as an interval throughout and every owner-dependent result is recomputed at the lower bound, the midpoint and the upper bound. Inclusion: released 2015 or later, owner-interval midpoint above 20,000 — a threshold aligned to SteamSpy's own bottom band rather than chosen freehand, which excludes games that flopped and tilts the sample toward titles that found an audience. Comparisons are rank-based (Mann-Whitney U with tie and continuity corrections, Cliff's delta as the effect size) because playtime is severely skewed. The effect size leads and the p-value follows, since at this sample size significance says little about magnitude. Within-genre results are pooled by pairwise weight across only those cells holding at least eight games of each model.
keyResults: Free-to-play median playtime 124 minutes against 530 for paid, across 1,198 free and 1,599 paid games with a usable reviewer sample. Cliff's delta -0.457 naive, -0.482 after genre adjustment across 58 genres. The three owner bounds agree to within 0.001, so the interval assumption — the most visible judgement call in the study — does not drive the conclusion.
businessInterpretation: Going free does not buy engagement on Steam, and the genre mix does not explain the shortfall. The two genres where free-to-play holds its own, Clicker and Idler, are designed around long low-intensity sessions, which suggests the model works where the game's loop already suits it rather than as a general lever. Price level is the stronger predictor: engagement climbs monotonically with price, more than tenfold from the cheapest band to the most expensive. The honest causal reading is that expensive games are not engaging because they are expensive — price is standing in for production budget, scope and buyer intent, none of which this data measures.
recommendations: Treat a free-to-play launch as a distribution decision rather than an engagement one: it buys reach, and this data gives no reason to expect it to buy time played. If engagement is the goal, the genre's session structure matters more than the price tag — the model earns its place in loops built for long passive play. Before converting an existing paid title, note that this study compares games as they are priced today, not as they launched, so it cannot speak to what conversion does to a specific title. That needs a before-and-after on the same game.
